title: ICE Holds Texas Store Worker After Jail Term Over Customer's Private Photos
excerpt: Raghul Anandakrishnan, 29, was convicted of attempted invasive visual recording after a customer said he tried to AirDrop her intimate photos to himself. ICE took him from the Travis County jail and will hold him pending immigration court proceedings.
body:
• Raghul Anandakrishnan, 29, is in ICE custody in Texas after serving a county jail sentence for attempted invasive visual recording.
  • ICE said it took custody of him directly from the Travis County jail and that he will remain detained pending immigration court proceedings.
  • The case began in June, when a customer at a Total Wireless store in Austin said an employee went through her iPhone and tried to AirDrop two intimate photographs to his own device.
  • ICE has not disclosed Anandakrishnan's immigration status or when he will appear before an immigration judge — the criminal conviction and the immigration case are separate processes.

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement has taken Raghul Anandakrishnan, a 29-year-old Indian-origin man, into custody in Texas after he completed a county jail sentence for attempted invasive visual recording, the agency said in a post on X on November 21. ICE said it took custody of him directly from the county jail and that he will remain in detention pending immigration court proceedings.

"Raghul Anandakrishnan served time in county jail in Texas after his conviction for attempted invasive visual recording. ICE took custody of him from the county jail. He'll remain in ICE custody pending immigration court proceedings."

— U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, on X

What happened at the Austin store

The case dates to June, when a woman told Austin police that an employee at a Total Wireless store at the Capital Plaza shopping centre had accessed her phone without her consent. According to court documents cited by FOX 7 Austin and reported by Jagran, the customer had come in to change her iPhone's network settings and gave Anandakrishnan her passcode so he could access the device. The affidavit says he opened her photo gallery and intentionally tried to send two nude photographs to himself through Apple's AirDrop feature. Anandakrishnan told investigators the transfer did not go through and that he returned the phone to the customer, according to the affidavit.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DgBQyK4l5sh/

Records from the Austin Police Department and Travis County court documents show Anandakrishnan was first lodged in the Travis County jail on June 7. He was initially charged with invasive visual recording, a state-jail felony, and breach of computer security, a Class B misdemeanour. He was later convicted of attempted invasive visual recording and served his sentence in the county jail before ICE took custody.

Two separate legal processes

The criminal case and the immigration case now run on separate tracks. The conviction is complete; what happens next is decided by an immigration court, which will consider his status and whether he is removable. As The Economic Times reported, ICE has not disclosed further details about Anandakrishnan's immigration status, the grounds for the proceedings, or when he will appear before an immigration judge.

Why this matters beyond one case

For non-citizens in the United States, a criminal conviction — even one that ends in a short county jail sentence rather than prison — can be the event that triggers immigration detention and removal proceedings. ICE routinely takes custody of people directly from local jails at the end of their sentences, which is what the agency says happened here. The practical lesson for diaspora readers is the one privacy lawyers repeat after cases like this: handing an unlocked phone, and its passcode, to a repair or retail counter means handing over everything on it. Where a store offers a supervised repair or a settings change that can be done in front of you, keep the device in sight — and never share the passcode.

What happens next

Anandakrishnan remains in ICE custody while his case moves through immigration court. No hearing date has been made public, and neither ICE nor the Travis County records cited in reporting have added detail about his status. This article will be updated if the agency releases more information.
